India is emerging as a major beneficiary of a significant shift in the global fashion supply chain, with international retailers including Zara, H&M, Marks & Spencer (M&S), and Celio reportedly moving some garment orders away from Bangladesh amid growing labour unrest, rising production costs, and factory disruptions.

Reports say global fashion brands diverted $254 million worth of orders from Bangladesh between November 1 and November 18, with most of the business moving to neighbouring India. The diverted orders accounted for nearly a tenth of the country's monthly apparel orders, according to three factory owners cited in the report.

Set in a beautiful, sunlit rural courtyard, this video captures the timeless art of cooking on a traditional clay chulha. As the rhythmic beat of the dholak plays in the background, a song celebrating this shared moment fills the air, creating a truly festive and heartwarming atmosphere.

The crisp sizzle of the flatbread on the hot iron tava and the sound of cheerful laughter bring the authentic essence of village life right to your screen. This short, vibrant clip is a tribute to heritage, connection, and the simple pleasures of preparing a meal together with love and music. Join us for a brief but deeply nourishing glimpse into this cherished cultural tradition of the Punjab region.

snippet.title: Fashola: Tinubu Will Win Lagos +INEC Chairman Can't Sway Results+Riggers Shouldn't Be Killed|OjyOkpe
snippet.description:
In an exclusive interview with Ojy Okpe, former Lagos State Governor Babatunde Raji Fashola, SAN, says he is confident President Bola Ahmed Tinubu will win Lagos in the January 16 presidential election — a state Peter Obi won in 2023.

The APC's South-West Zonal Coordinator for Stakeholders' Mobilisation insists the INEC Chairman cannot influence election results. He says election riggers should not be given the death sentence, but that Nigeria needs to make an example of political offenders.

In this interview, Fashola also:
* Says he will not run for public office again, describing his years in government as a privilege
* Disagrees that the APC caused the cost of living crisis, blaming Covid and the wars in Ukraine and Iran
* Calls fuel subsidy an unsustainable model
* Defends his record as Power Minister, saying 11 million people were connected to electricity during his time
* Says he is optimistic about a second Tinubu term, based on the President's record as Lagos Governor
* Credits President Tinubu with "taming the Atlantic"
* Pays tribute to governorship aspirant Funsho Williams, 20 years after his murder

snippet.title: The Aral Sea Is Coming Back
snippet.description:
Follow the link and purchase the book with my Promo Code: LOOKING10 👉 https://mdsh.io/7r4hehevku

What if I told you that a genuine inland sea has almost completely disappeared from the face of the earth in the space of sixty years? 

Lost amid the deserts of Central Asia, the Aral Sea was far more than just a sea. It was an immense salt lake, a gigantic basin draining water from the region's entire catchment. In the 1960s, this expanse teemed with life and supported as many as sixty thousand fishermen. Its waves stretched to the horizon. At the time, no one could have imagined that such a mass of water might lose ninety percent of its surface area in six decades. But that was without reckoning with the intensive agricultural policies that would rapidly destroy this ecosystem.

Today, the unthinkable has happened. The bed of the former sea is now nothing more than a desert of sand and salt known as the Aralkum, a landscape strewn with the wrecks of rusting trawlers. This extraordinarily rapid desiccation remains one of the worst ecological disasters of our time, often dubbed the "Chernobyl of Central Asia". It's also a brutal reminder that our resources are not infinite and that poor water management can wipe a sea off the map.

But to truly understand the fate of the Aral Sea, it's not enough to simply contemplate its remains. We must go back to the source of the problem and understand why, against all expectations, a glimmer of hope remains. Thanks to international initiatives and the construction of a dam, part of its waters have been saved in the north, while the great sea in the south is doomed to disappear. 

Where does the water that once reached these desolate shores vanish to? The answer lies in the arid lands of Central Asia, along the two mighty rivers that have enabled this region to prosper for centuries. The Amu Darya, which supplies the south, and the Syr Darya, which irrigates the north. Two major waterways that are now overexploited, particularly for the production of the region's white gold, cotton.

In this episode of Looking For, we're going to cross Central Asia to unravel the mystery of this sacrificed sea, while also discovering the recent projects that are now attempting to save it. From the vertiginous glaciers of the Pamirs to the immense irrigated fields, this is the story of the Aral Sea.
